passage:
Day 1, Monday: “I'll start when I feel like it,” Vaibhav told his sister Trisha, and lay on the sofa with a comic. The evening drifted by. He drew a little, ate a banana, watched the ceiling fan and went to sleep with the spelling list untouched.

Day 3, Wednesday: Same sentence, same sofa. The feeling did not come.

Day 5, Friday, nine o'clock at night: The test was next morning. Vaibhav grumbled, opened the notebook only because there was nothing else left to try, and copied out the first five words. By the tenth word, he had forgotten he wasn't in the mood.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav tell his sister Trisha?
qa.a: Vaibhav told Trisha, “I'll start when I feel like it.”

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav open the notebook on Friday night?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt cornered and a bit grumpy, because the test was the next morning and waiting had not brought the feeling.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav try on Monday instead of waiting?
qa.a: Open the notebook and copy out just the first five words, and let the mood catch up after he has started.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel watching Vaibhav wait for the mood?
qa.a: Trisha probably feels a mix of patience and worry, having heard the same sentence twice without the spelling list moving.

grounding: A child waits until he feels like it, drifts through evenings, and finds motivation only after starting.

passage: “Simran, you say you'll begin when you feel like it. Listen. I'm Himani, and when I was ten, I said the same, every evening, about my sums. I'd sit with the book shut and think, the mood will come. It came at bedtime, and then only as guilt. The third night before a test I was up until eleven with a wet cloth on my forehead to stay awake. Then one day my teacher said, 'Do the first sum and tell me how you feel.' I did it, grumbling. The second sum came easier. By the fifth, I wanted to go on. The mood didn't arrive first, child. It arrived after.”

qa.q: How old was Himani when saying the same sentence?
qa.a: Himani was ten years old.

qa.q: What did the young Himani expect while sitting with the book shut?
qa.a: Himani expected the mood to come and felt hopeful and waiting, but it only came at bedtime as guilt.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Himani's evenings?
qa.a: The teacher asked Himani to do the first sum and say how it felt, and by the fifth sum Himani wanted to go on.

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt asking Himani to do just the first sum?
qa.a: The teacher probably felt patient and hopeful, and was inviting Himani to find out from experience rather than being told.

grounding: A child waits to feel like starting homework, drifts, and learns that the feeling arrives after starting.

passage: There was half an hour before tuition, and the builders next door had started drilling. Lavanya stared at the chemistry chapter as if it were a dentist's chair. Her throat felt tight. Everything else suddenly looked interesting: the pen stand, the fan blade, a crack in the wall. Her sister Ira looked in and said, “Just ten minutes, open it, read one page. If it's still terrible, stop.” Lavanya groaned, but she opened the book and put a finger under the first line. Five minutes in, the drilling faded. Nine minutes in, she was underlining. When the timer buzzed she looked surprised and turned the page anyway.

qa.q: How long before tuition did the drilling start?
qa.a: The drilling started half an hour before tuition.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling as she stared at the chapter?
qa.a: Lavanya felt dread and tension, shown by the tight throat and her eyes wandering to other things.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's experience suggest about getting past the first minutes of revising?
qa.a: Open the book and give it ten minutes: the first minutes were the hard part, and after five the drilling faded and after nine Lavanya was underlining, so the dread was about the entrance more than the work.

qa.q: How might Ira be feeling when suggesting ten minutes?
qa.a: Ira is probably sympathetic and practical, offering a small trial and permission to stop so that starting feels safe for Lavanya.

grounding: A teenager dreads revising, but once the book is open the resistance fades.

passage: Sunday morning, and Karthik had been standing by the bookshelf for a quarter of an hour. Geography revision. Just thinking of the atlas made him tired. He made tea, checked the balcony, wiped the table. His mother Alka, chopping onions, said nothing. Finally he sat, set the phone timer for ten minutes, opened the atlas to the rivers map and traced the first river with a pencil. It wasn't so bad. He traced the second one. When the timer sounded, he glanced up, faintly puzzled. Where had the dread gone? It had been so heavy at the shelf, and it was almost nothing at the table. He kept the timer running for another ten.

qa.q: Who was chopping onions in the kitchen?
qa.a: Karthik's mother Alka was chopping onions.

qa.q: Why did Karthik make tea and wipe the table before sitting down?
qa.a: Karthik was dreading the atlas and delaying, since the thought of it made him tired.

qa.q: What was Karthik puzzled about when the timer sounded?
qa.a: Karthik was puzzled that the dread had almost vanished; it had been heavy at the shelf but small at the table.

qa.q: How might Alka see Karthik's fifteen minutes by the shelf?
qa.a: Alka watches quietly and probably feels patient and a little amused, giving Karthik room to start on his own.

grounding: A teenager finds revision unbearable to face, but after ten minutes with the book open the resistance largely fades.

passage:
“I can't do this essay. I don't even want to look at it,” Kashish said, flopping onto the bed.
“Five minutes,” said Irfan, her older brother, from the desk chair.
“Five minutes for what?”
“Open the file. Write one sentence. Any sentence. Then you're allowed to stop.”
“Allowed?”
“Truly. I'll even take the phone.” Irfan held out a hand.
Kashish gave it a look, then sat up, opened the laptop and typed: The river changed the town. It was terrible. She typed a second sentence, a bit better.
“Five minutes are over,” said Irfan.
“Shh,” said Kashish. “I'm in the middle of a paragraph.”

qa.q: What did Irfan ask Kashish to write in five minutes?
qa.a: Irfan asked Kashish to open the file and write one sentence, any sentence, and then stop.

qa.q: What did Kashish feel when flopping onto the bed?
qa.a: Kashish felt reluctant and dreading the essay, saying she couldn't do it and didn't even want to look at it.

qa.q: What made the tiny start work for Kashish?
qa.a: Permission to stop after five minutes made starting feel safe, and the first bad sentence pulled a second and then a paragraph.

qa.q: How does Irfan seem to feel about Kashish and the essay?
qa.a: Irfan seems patient and supportive, offering a small commitment and even taking the phone away, without pushing or lecturing.

grounding: A wise approach commits to five minutes, writing one sentence, with permission to stop; motion creates momentum.

passage: In class ten, geometry was my monster. My cousin Dolma, two years older, noticed me circling the desk the way you circle a dog you don't trust. “Don't do the chapter,” Dolma said. “Do five minutes. Lay out the compass, the ruler and the pencil, and open the book to the first theorem. Then, if you want, close it.” I laughed, because it sounded too small to matter. But when the geometry box was open and the pencil sharpened, drawing the first triangle seemed only natural. I didn't close the book that day, or the next. I still lay out my tools before any dreaded job. — Manoj

qa.q: Who suggested the five-minute start?
qa.a: Manoj's cousin Dolma suggested it.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel about geometry in class ten?
qa.a: Manoj felt wary and dreading it, like circling a dog one doesn't trust, and laughed at first because five minutes sounded too small to matter.

qa.q: What did Dolma suggest laying out, and what was the effect?
qa.a: Dolma suggested laying out the compass, the ruler and the pencil and opening the first theorem; with the tools ready, drawing the first triangle felt natural.

qa.q: How might Dolma have felt suggesting such a small step?
qa.a: Dolma was probably gentle and understanding, since Dolma noticed the circling and gave permission to close the book afterwards.

grounding: A wise approach is to commit to five minutes and lay out the tools; motion creates momentum and permission to stop makes starting safe.

passage: I'm Darshan and I share a flat with Jagdish. For three weeks I watched Jagdish wait for the right conditions to write the thesis chapter. First it was the desk: too cluttered, so Jagdish tidied it and bought a new lamp. Then it was time: “I need a whole free day.” The free day came on Sunday, and Jagdish said the mood wasn't right. Then it was a new pen. The desk stayed clear and the document stayed empty. I don't know what was going on in Jagdish's mind, maybe worry about the chapter being not good enough. When I asked, the answer was, “Once everything is set, it will flow.” Everything never seemed to be set.

qa.q: What did Jagdish buy while waiting for the right conditions?
qa.a: Jagdish bought a new lamp and a new pen.

qa.q: What might Jagdish be feeling behind “once everything is set, it will flow”?
qa.a: Jagdish may be anxious or afraid the chapter won't be good enough, though Darshan cannot be sure; the waiting looks like a polite name for postponing.

qa.q: What could Jagdish try to break the pattern?
qa.a: Sit down at the ordinary messy desk for a set half hour and write a rough page, without waiting for the day, the mood or a new pen.

qa.q: How does Darshan see Jagdish's waiting?
qa.a: Darshan is watchful and a little worried, noticing the tidy desk and empty document and guessing at worry rather than laziness.

grounding: A young adult waits for a clear desk, a free day and the right mood before starting a thesis chapter.

passage:
Day 1: Chinmay cleared the desk, put a fresh notebook beside the laptop and said to Uma in the library, “I'll begin the chapter tomorrow, when I've got the whole morning.”

Day 9: The whole morning had not appeared. Chinmay now said, “Saturday, when the hostel is empty and quiet.” Saturday, a pigeon cooed outside, and someone played music down the corridor, and the quiet wasn't right.

Day 20: Uma found Chinmay on a crowded bus with a phone open on a note app, typing in half-sentences. “Two hundred words,” Chinmay said, pleased, not looking up. “On a bus.”

qa.q: Where did Chinmay tell Uma about beginning the chapter?
qa.a: Chinmay told Uma in the library.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay keep moving the start date?
qa.a: Chinmay felt uneasy about the big chapter and relieved each time the start moved, so waiting for perfect conditions became a way of postponing it.

qa.q: What happened on Day 20 that had not happened before?
qa.a: Chinmay wrote two hundred words on a crowded bus, in half-sentences on a phone, without a clear desk, a whole morning or quiet.

qa.q: How might Uma feel finding Chinmay typing on the bus?
qa.a: Uma is probably surprised and glad, having seen the waiting for weeks and now seeing real words appear.

grounding: A young adult waits for a clear desk, a full day and quiet before a thesis chapter, and begins only when conditions are imperfect.

passage: The moving van was booked for Saturday, and Yash had come over to help Abhinav pack. The flat looked frozen. Boxes lay unfolded, the kitchen sink was full, and a form for a job application, once urgent, still sat unopened on the table. Abhinav had barely started anything in weeks, and it wasn't like Abhinav to be this flat. Yash didn't lecture about discipline. Yash sat down, made two cups of tea, and said, “You haven't seemed like yourself for a while. I'm worried. Would it help to talk to a doctor or a counsellor? I can find a number and come with you.” Abhinav was silent, then nodded a little. “Maybe,” Abhinav said. Yash folded the first box.

qa.q: What day was the moving van booked for?
qa.a: The moving van was booked for Saturday.

qa.q: Why did Yash choose to sit down with tea instead of lecturing?
qa.a: Yash felt worried about Abhinav and sensed that a lecture on discipline would not help, so wanted to show care and offer practical company.

qa.q: What did Yash choose to do instead of lecturing about discipline?
qa.a: Yash made tea, said honestly that Yash was worried, suggested a doctor or counsellor and offered to find a number and go along.

qa.q: What might Abhinav be feeling behind the silence and the small nod?
qa.a: Abhinav seems flat and worn out, perhaps relieved to be noticed and less alone, and the tentative “Maybe” suggests hope mixed with hesitation.

grounding: Someone notices a person unable to start anything for weeks and gently suggests a doctor or counsellor instead of lecturing.

passage:
On Thursday, Shalini stopped by Hafsa's desk with two cups of tea and found the screen showing the same spreadsheet as last week. Weeks of half-finished reports, unanswered mails and missed lunches. Hafsa, once the quickest in the team, now stared at the cursor.
“I'm not here to check up on the work,” Shalini said. “I'm here because you don't seem like yourself.”
Hafsa shrugged. “I just can't start anything.”
“That sounds heavy. Have you thought about talking to a doctor or counsellor? I can sit with you while you find a number.”
Hafsa looked at the tea. “Maybe.”
“No rush today. I'll ask again next week.”

qa.q: What was on Hafsa's screen when Shalini stopped by?
qa.a: The screen showed the same spreadsheet as last week.

qa.q: Why did Shalini say “I'm not here to check up on the work”?
qa.a: Shalini felt worried about Hafsa and wanted to make clear that the visit was about care, not about pressure over deadlines.

qa.q: What did Shalini offer, and what did Shalini avoid saying?
qa.a: Shalini offered to sit with Hafsa while finding a doctor or counsellor's number, and did not lecture about work or discipline.

qa.q: What might Hafsa be feeling when saying “I just can't start anything”?
qa.a: Hafsa feels stuck and heavy, unable to get going despite wanting to, which is more than ordinary laziness; being asked rather than told may leave room to say yes in Hafsa's own time.

grounding: Someone notices a person unable to start anything beyond ordinary laziness and gently suggests a doctor or counsellor.

passage:
Gautam: no motivation at all today. can't make myself open the report
Vinita: 🙂 I don't wait for motivation anymore
Gautam: how
Vinita: I have a routine. 9:30, laptop open, first paragraph, twenty minutes. every day, even flat days
Gautam: what if I'm just not feeling it
Vinita: then you do it not feeling it. the feeling usually turns up around minute ten
Gautam: hm. ok. twenty minutes
Vinita: message me after
Gautam: (25 min later) ok. I did three paragraphs and forgot to check the time
Vinita: 🎉 see. motivation is what starting gives you

qa.q: What time is Vinita's routine?

qa.q: How does Gautam feel at the start of the chat?
qa.a: Gautam feels flat and unmotivated, with no drive to even open the report.

qa.q: What did the routine do for Gautam that waiting had not done?
qa.a: Gautam started without feeling like it and wrote three paragraphs, forgetting the time, so the motivation came after starting.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel when Gautam reports three paragraphs?

passage: Naveen unlocked the tailoring shop's shutter at eight every morning, even on the days when nothing inside him wanted to. This morning the road was wet, the festival was over, and his shoulders felt heavy. His apprentice Harsha, arriving, half-expected him to sit and stare at the rain. Instead Naveen swept the floor, laid out the chalk and the shears, and threaded the machine. “Some days I don't want to,” he said, matter of fact. “The routine does it for me.” By ten a customer had come in for a blouse fitting, and the whirr of the machine had eased the heaviness. Harsha watched him cut the first cloth and stayed quiet.

qa.q: At what time did Naveen unlock the shutter every morning?
qa.a: Naveen unlocked the tailoring shop's shutter at eight every morning.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel this morning, and how do we know?
qa.a: Naveen felt heavy and unmotivated, shown by the wet road, the heavy shoulders and his saying some days he doesn't want to.

qa.q: What did Naveen do, in order, that got him going?
qa.a: Naveen swept the floor, laid out the chalk and shears and threaded the machine, and by ten the first customer's fitting had eased the heaviness.

qa.q: What might Harsha be thinking while watching Naveen cut the first cloth?
qa.a: Harsha is probably impressed and thoughtful, having expected Naveen to sit and stare at the rain, and quietly learns from what Naveen does.

grounding: A worker treats motivation as a result of starting and follows a fixed routine on flat days.

passage: On Monday the teacher said the model project was due in two weeks, and Harsha felt only a warm wave of relief. Two weeks! That was almost forever. Zainab, at the next desk, was already planning her volcano. Harsha drew spaceships in the margin instead. Days went by, one, four, seven. At the end of the first week Harsha thought, still lots of time. On the tenth day, a small pinch in the stomach. On the twelfth, Harsha realised the day after tomorrow was tomorrow. The last two evenings were a blur of glue, cardboard and a very tired mother, and the model went in slightly lopsided but finished.

qa.q: How long did the teacher give for the model project?
qa.a: The teacher said the model project was due in two weeks.

qa.q: What did Harsha feel when the teacher announced two weeks?
qa.a: Harsha felt a warm wave of relief, sure there was almost forever, so the deadline had no emotional weight yet.

qa.q: What could Harsha do at the start of the two weeks to avoid the last-two-day rush?
qa.a: Choose a small first job for the first week, like making a sketch or listing the materials, and write a mid-way date on the calendar.

qa.q: How might Zainab see the difference between the two of them?
qa.a: Zainab, already planning a volcano, probably sees that the project has become real for Zainab and may wonder why Harsha is drawing spaceships.

grounding: A child told a project is due in two weeks feels there is endless time and does nothing until the last two days.

passage:
“It's due in two weeks, Papa. That's ages,” said Tanvir, not looking up from the tablet.
“Two weeks is fourteen days,” said Baljeet. “What will you do on the first one?”
“Nothing. I'll do it later.”
Days passed. On the twelfth evening, Baljeet found Tanvir sitting on the floor with cardboard, scissors and no plan.
“How did that happen?” Baljeet asked.
“I thought I had so much time. Two weeks was so long.”
“And now?”
“Now it's two days.” Tanvir's voice cracked. “Can you help me hold this?”
Baljeet knelt on the floor beside him. “I'll hold it. You decide what goes where.”

qa.q: On which evening did Baljeet find Tanvir with cardboard and scissors?
qa.a: Baljeet found Tanvir on the twelfth evening.

qa.q: How does Tanvir feel when the voice cracks and the project is two days away?
qa.a: Tanvir feels panicky and ashamed, and his voice cracking shows the deadline has finally become real.

qa.q: What could Baljeet and Tanvir do so the next project does not end this way?
qa.a: Write the due date on the wall, and split the two weeks into small steps with a first task on day one.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel kneeling beside Tanvir?
qa.a: Baljeet is probably concerned and patient, willing to hold the cardboard but leaving the decisions to Tanvir.

grounding: A child told a project is due in two weeks feels there is endless time and begins only in the last days.

passage:
Anjali: So how did the history project go?
Wasim: Okay, don't laugh. It was due Friday at eight in the morning. On Thursday evening I still hadn't started the poster. And honestly, I felt fine. Around ten at night, the panic kicked in, and then something clicked. I was flying, cutting, gluing, writing captions in one long burst. I slept three hours. In the morning my hands were shaking and my eyes felt sandy, but I told myself, look, I can do it in one night. It felt like proof I was good. Then the teacher pointed out two wrong dates and a caption pasted upside down. I said “I know” and I didn't know what else to say. 😅

qa.q: At what time on Friday was the project due?
qa.a: The project was due on Friday at eight in the morning.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel after finishing the poster in one night?
qa.a: Wasim felt proud and excited, seeing it as proof of ability, though tired and shaky.

qa.q: What was the cost of the night-before rush?
qa.a: Wasim slept only three hours and handed in a poster with two wrong dates and an upside-down caption.

qa.q: How might Anjali react to hearing the story?
qa.a: Anjali is probably curious and sympathetic, and may notice that the feeling of proof came from pressure rather than from the poster's quality.

grounding: A teenager works frantically the night before a submission and delivers something rushed, taking the adrenaline as proof of ability.

passage: I'm Chaitanya. I live across the corridor from Vijay, and on Sunday night I saw Vijay's light on until nearly three. Through the door I could hear frantic typing, then a groan, then a whispered “no, no, no.” In the morning Vijay came out with red eyes, holding a printout, and said cheerfully, “Finished the whole report in one night. I work best like this.” It seemed a proud sentence, though I couldn't tell whether Vijay believed it or wished to. Later I heard the report came back with a comment about missing sections and a rushed conclusion. Vijay didn't mention the comment and asked if anyone had a spare pen.

qa.q: Until what time was Vijay's light on on Sunday night?
qa.a: Vijay's light was on until nearly three.

qa.q: What might Vijay have felt when saying “I work best like this”?
qa.a: Vijay may have been proud and relieved after the rush, yet perhaps also tired and hoping to believe it, but Chaitanya cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Vijay try before the next report to avoid a three a.m. finish?
qa.a: Start a few days earlier with a small piece each evening, so the final night is for checking, not creating.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya interpret Vijay's cheerful announcement?
qa.a: Chaitanya notices the pride but is not sure whether Vijay believes it, since the red eyes and the groans suggest a harder night.

grounding: A teenager works frantically the night before a submission and takes the adrenaline as proof of ability, seen by someone across the corridor.

subtype: Pressure as fuel and its cost [Actor]
passage: “Ankita, sit. You told your friends that a deadline sharpens you, and I, Bhupen, said it too, once. Third year of engineering, every project done on the last night, and it mostly worked, so I believed it. For my final thesis I planned the same: start on the night before the deadline. Two days before, I woke with a high fever and a body that would not stand. There was no last night to use. I lay in bed, frantic, while my roommate carried water to me. The department was kind about an extension, but the work I finally submitted was thin, and it taught me that all those last nights had only been luck, not a skill.”

qa.q: In which year of engineering did Bhupen begin doing projects on the last night?
qa.a: In the third year of engineering, Bhupen did every project on the last night.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel lying in bed with a fever two days before the deadline?
qa.a: Bhupen felt frantic and helpless, because the plan depended on a last night that could not now be used.

qa.q: What went wrong with Bhupen's plan, and what did it reveal?
qa.a: An unexpected fever ruined the plan of starting the night before, and the thin thesis showed that leaving things late had been luck, not a skill.

qa.q: How might Ankita react to hearing Bhupen's story?
qa.a: Ankita may feel startled and reflective, since Ankita also trusts deadlines to sharpen the mind, and might now see the risk in the habit.

grounding: A college student works best under pressure and leaves things to the last day, but one illness breaks the plan.

subtype: Pressure as fuel and its cost [Actor]
passage: “Nine hours left,” Elizabeth said, tapping her laptop. “I work best under pressure.” Nazia, her roommate, glanced at the clock and at the empty document. At 2 pm the campus internet crashed. Elizabeth ran to the library, found every table taken, and typed on the staircase with the laptop on her knees. At 4:20 she attached the file, but the charts were missing, and the conclusion ended mid-sentence. She submitted at 4:58 anyway, and lay on her bed, exhausted, with a headache. “It'll be fine,” she said. But she had not slept the night before, and she knew the essay was not what she had meant it to be. Nazia handed her some water and said nothing.

qa.q: At what time did the campus internet crash?
qa.a: The campus internet crashed at 2 pm.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when she said “It'll be fine”?
qa.a: Elizabeth was exhausted and uneasy, trying to reassure herself, while knowing the essay was not what she had meant.

qa.q: What went wrong on the last day, and what did it show about working under pressure?
qa.a: The internet crash and a crowded library left no slack, and the essay went in with missing charts and an unfinished conclusion, showing the habit has costs.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel while handing over water and saying nothing?
qa.a: Nazia is probably sympathetic and a little worried, having seen the pattern, but chooses kindness over saying “I told you so”.

grounding: A college student who says they work best under pressure leaves work to the last day, and quality and sleep suffer.

passage:
Mridul: So your dissertation was due on the twentieth. When did you finish?
Hrithik: The rough draft was done on the tenth. I always set my own date about ten days before the real one. I write it in my calendar in a different colour so it feels real.
Mridul: And then?
Hrithik: On the sixteenth the university's website went down for a whole day, the printer at the library broke, and my supervisor was ill. Everyone else in my class panicked. I was already reading my draft for the third time, changing words, fixing the introduction. I submitted it on the eighteenth. Honestly, the last days were the nicest part.

qa.q: On what date was the rough draft done?
qa.a: The rough draft was done on the tenth.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik feel calm while others panicked?
qa.a: Hrithik felt steady and content, because the draft was already finished and the last days were for improving, not scrambling.

qa.q: What did Hrithik do that gave room for surprises?
qa.a: Hrithik set a personal date about ten days before the real deadline, wrote it in a different colour and finished the rough draft early.

qa.q: How might Mridul be feeling while listening?
qa.a: Mridul seems curious and impressed, and is asking questions to find out how Hrithik managed to finish so calmly.

grounding: A wise worker sets personal milestones ahead of the real date and finishes a rough draft early, leaving room for surprises.

passage: I'm Jaya, and I share the internship desk with Pradeep. Our report was due on the thirtieth, but Pradeep announced a different date: “Rough draft by the twentieth.” It was written on a sticky note above the monitor. On the twentieth, Pradeep printed a messy draft with gaps and read it over lunch. In the last week, when the rest of us panicked because the manager suddenly asked for extra charts, Pradeep just added them, calmly, and spent two days tidying the language. I don't know how Pradeep felt inside; there was no visible stress. I do remember the quiet on the twenty-ninth, when Pradeep was already having tea.

qa.q: What was written on the sticky note above the monitor?
qa.a: The sticky note said, “Rough draft by the twentieth.”

qa.q: How might Pradeep have felt on the twenty-ninth?
qa.a: Pradeep seemed calm and unhurried, having tea while others were busy, though Jaya cannot know the inner state for certain.

qa.q: What did the early draft make possible when the manager asked for extra charts?
qa.a: Pradeep could add the charts calmly and spend two days tidying the language, since the main work was already done.

qa.q: How does Jaya see Pradeep's early date compared with the others' plans?
qa.a: Jaya notices that the others panicked at the extra charts, and probably feels a mix of admiration and a wish to do the same next time.

grounding: A wise worker sets an earlier personal milestone and finishes a rough draft early, leaving room for surprises.
